concept.body: Thales' theorem: an inscribed angle opening onto a DIAMETER is exactly 90° — the diameter's arc is a 180° semicircle, and inscribed angles take half. Converse: if an inscribed angle is 90°, its chord is a diameter. In the resulting right triangle the diameter is the hypotenuse and the two acute angles are complements.

explanationVariants: The diameter's arc is 180°; the inscribed angle is half: 90°, wherever P sits.

widget.prompt: P is a point on a circle; MN is a diameter. Angle MPN = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° is the semicircle arc — P sees it at half: 90°.
60° would suit a 120° arc — a diameter always spans 180°: 90°.

steps.body: Point the inscribed angle at a **diameter** and the theorem sings: the diameter's arc is a semicircle, 180°, so the inscribed angle is half of that — **exactly 90°, from anywhere on the circle**. That's Thales' theorem, arguably the oldest proved statement in mathematics.

explanationVariants: AB is a diameter, so its arc is 180° and any inscribed angle on it is 90°.
Thales: diameter seen from the rim = right angle, always.

widget.prompt: AB is a diameter of a circle and C is any other point on the circle. Angle ACB measures ?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° is the semicircle ARC — the inscribed angle halves it: 90°.
45 halves twice — one halving of 180° lands at 90°.
60° would need a 120° arc — a diameter's arc is a full 180°: 90°.

steps.body: Thales turns every such triangle into a RIGHT triangle whose hypotenuse is the diameter — so the whole right-triangle toolkit (Pythagoras, the trig course) boards the circle. And the two remaining angles? They must complete 180° past the right angle: complements of each other.

explanationVariants: Angles sum to 180; with 90° spoken for, the acute pair totals 90: the other is 90 − 28 = 62°.

widget.prompt: Triangle ABC is inscribed with AB a diameter. Angle A = 28°. Find angle B.

commonErrors.feedback: 28° copies angle A — the acute pair are complements, not twins: 90 − 28 = 62°.
152 = 180 − 28 forgets the right angle at C already holds 90°: the pair shares only 90. 62°.
118 = 90 + 28 adds instead of completing — angle B finishes the 90: 62°.

steps.body: Push the arc all the way to a semicircle.

widget.prompt: Make the angle at P a right angle. Watch what the chord AB becomes when you get there.
widget.successFeedback: At 180° of arc, AB is a diameter and the angle at P is exactly 90°. Thales' theorem is not a separate fact — it is the inscribed-angle rule at its one special arc. And P can still slide anywhere: every point on the semicircle sees the diameter at a right angle.
widget.lowFeedback: Under 90° at P. The angle is half the arc, so you need the arc to reach a full 180°.
widget.highFeedback: Past 90°, which means the arc has gone beyond a semicircle and AB is no longer a diameter.

predict.prompt: The arc starts at 120°. The inscribed angle that watches it measures…
predict.reveal: It reads 60° — half. Only the CENTRAL angle matches its arc; every angle whose vertex sits on the circle gets exactly half, and dragging the arc will hold that ratio pinned.

cml.actionGoal: Move points on a circle while arc, central-angle, and inscribed-angle measures update together.

widget.prompt: A carpenter slides a square (a rigid 90° corner) so both edges touch two fixed nails, marking where the corner sits. What does the corner trace, and why?

options.label: A circle through the nails — by the converse, the corner always sees the nail-segment as a diameter
options.feedback: Every 90° view of segment AB sits on the circle with AB as diameter — the tool literally draws Thales' converse.

options.label: A straight line parallel to the nails
options.feedback: A line would keep a constant distance, but the corner's DISTANCE varies — what stays constant is the 90° view: a circle.

options.label: An ellipse with the nails as foci
options.feedback: Ellipses keep a distance SUM constant — this tool keeps an ANGLE constant at 90°, which is Thales' circle.

options.label: Nothing recognizable
options.feedback: It's exactly the semicircle on the nail segment — machinists have used this circle-finding trick for centuries.

explanationVariants: Thales makes the legs 10 and 24 a right pair, so the hypotenuse-diameter is √(100 + 576) = 26.
Pythagoras on the Thales triangle: √676 = 26 — the 5-12-13 triple, doubled.

widget.prompt: A triangle inscribed on a diameter has legs 10 and 24. Find the DIAMETER.

commonErrors.feedback: 34 = 10 + 24 adds the legs — the diameter is the HYPOTENUSE: √(10² + 24²) = 26.
13 is the RADIUS — the diameter doubles it: 26.
21.82 ≈ √(576 − 100) subtracts squares — both givens are LEGS, so add: 26.

hints: The right angle at C certifies (converse!) that AB is a diameter.
Pythagoras prices AB from the legs 9 and 12.
The radius is HALF the diameter.
explanationVariants: AB = √(81 + 144) = 15 (the 3-4-5 family), so the radius is 7.5.

widget.prompt: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle with a right angle at C, and legs AC = 9, BC = 12. Find the circle's RADIUS.

commonErrors.feedback: 15 is the diameter AB — the radius halves it: 7.5.
10.5 = (9 + 12)/2 averages the legs — first Pythagoras (15), then halve: 7.5.
6 ≈ half of √(144 − 81) subtracts squares — the legs ADD: √225 = 15, radius 7.5.

takeaways: Thales: any inscribed angle on a diameter is 90° (half the 180° semicircle).
Converse: a 90° inscribed angle forces its chord to BE a diameter — hypotenuse through the center.
The acute pair are complements, and Pythagoras prices the diameter from the legs.
